The Shadow That Reached the Mark Too Soon

提早碰到刻线的影子 · 643 词 · 8 段 · 首次出现的目标词加粗

1A science club installed a vertical rod in a schoolyard to measure the sun's shadow. Its forecast said the shortest shadow would touch a line at noon. It arrived eleven minutes early. A student named Ian thought gravity had tilted the rod. Another blamed a clock. The teacher asked them to record the direction and length of the shadow through a full afternoon. A single reading could reveal a discrepancy. It could not yet identify the variable that caused it.

2Ian drew a horizontal scale in centimeters and added millimeter marks. A stiff bracket held the rod. Its diameter matched the plan, and a weight gave the direction of gravity. Its inclination had not changed. A digital clock confirmed the minute precisely. The difference was attributable to an assumption in the printed design. It used a line for another geographic position. The school's actual location was farther east. The shadow's direction would correspond to a different time, even under equivalent weather.

3A globe showed Earth's axis and spherical shape. In astronomy those features could explain a proportional shift over a day. The class compared both locations on a circular chart. The towns' separation represented a small proportion of the whole sphere. With parallel lines and basic geometry Ian derived an approximate time shift. He used a ratio rather than guess how far an invisible beam had moved. The simple calculation gave a tangible indication of how a small spatial difference could produce a significant result.

4The noon shadow generally varied with the date. A fairly small shift could still matter. A diagram of Earth's orbit distinguished local measurement from a prediction about planetary motion. An astronomer might use a telescope to study a distant planet. Here the scientific method required a stable rod and a series of comparable records. The shadow did not decrease in a perfectly linear way. The club could quantify a trend after an adequate span rather than treat a mere coincidence as a consequence of the season.

5A first graph showed a sudden drop after a cloudy afternoon. Ian had written a precise number beside a faint edge. His partner asked what that implied about accuracy. They set a tolerable range and marked exceptional conditions. A wet patch could reflect light and make the line appear to fluctuate. A marginal change was no cause for optimism or a pessimistic forecast. Their estimation needed to show which readings were doubtful and which gave a coherent pattern.

6The report also stated the duration of the test and the overall variation. A pupil wanted to calculate the likelihood of an exact result. The teacher gave him a range. Calculating positive and negative error was a reasonable first step. A noticeable lag might come from the clock, whereas a lasting shift might reflect an orbital factor. Those explanations made the graph more useful under less than ideal conditions.

7The club used the new scale to predict where the shadow would fall the following week. A teacher wanted a single digit for the notice. Ian gave him an interval instead. He explained that temperature and clouds could affect what a pupil saw, while astronomical position determined the expected direction. The prediction included enough margin for a faint edge. When the next class made a comparison, its reading lay inside the expected range. The result was more useful than a guess that happened to match one number.

8Ian showed a visitor both marks. A typical reading fell close to the new one. In extreme weather, fog made its position uncertain. A thermometer gave the temperature in degrees centigrade, but an atmospheric change did not account for the whole shift. The visitor could see how an astronomical phenomenon and climatic conditions affected different parts of the observation. He circled a reading with an unusually large fluctuation and wrote what he would check during the next investigation.

提早碰到刻线的影子

按英文段落顺序对照阅读

1科学社在校园里竖一根杆量日影。按原先预报，正午最短的影子会碰到一条线，结果提前了十一分钟。学生伊恩怀疑杆子受重力影响歪了，另一人怪钟不准。老师请他们记录整个下午影子的方向和长度。一次读数能发现差异，还不能确定是哪个因素造成的。

2伊恩画了水平的厘米刻度，又加上毫米线。一只硬支架固定着杆，杆的直径合图纸，用垂重也能看出重力方向。倾斜度没有变，电子钟确认时间也准。原来偏差来自图纸上的一个假设。图纸为另一个地理位置画了线，学校实际在更东边。即使天气相同，影子朝那个方向的时刻也会变。

3地球仪展示了地轴和球形外观。天文学可以用这些特点解释一天里的比例变化。全班在圆形图上标两个地点。两镇的间距只是整个球体的一小部分。伊恩用平行线和基本几何求出大致的时间差，用比例说明一束看不见的光会移到哪儿。简单计算让人看清，一个小小的空间差异也能产生明显结果。

4正午的影子通常还随日期变化，变化很小也可能有影响。地球轨道图把本地测量和对行星运动的预测区分开。天文学家可能用望远镜看遥远行星。这里需要的是一根稳定的杆和一系列可比较的读数。影长不会完全按直线比例缩短。记录够久，社团才能量出趋势，避免把偶然相同的两天当成季节规律。

5第一张图在一个阴天下午突然下降。影子的边缘很淡，伊恩还是写了一个精确数字。同伴问，这对准确性意味着什么。他们改写可容许的范围，再标出特殊条件。一片湿地能反光，让线看起来波动。小小的偏差不必引出过度乐观或悲观。估计需要说明，哪些数据不确定，哪些能连成一致的变化。

6报告还写了试验持续多久和整体变化。一位学生想算某个准确结果出现的概率，老师给他一个范围。先算正负误差，是合理的第一步。显著的迟滞也许来自钟表，持续偏移则可能和轨道有关。即使条件不理想，有这些说明，图也更好用。

7社团用新刻度预测下周影子的位置。老师想在公告上写一个数，伊恩给了一个区间。他解释说，气温和云会改变人看得清多少，天体位置才决定预期方向。预报留了余量给模糊的边缘。下个班来比较，读数确实落在区间内。这样的结果比碰巧猜中一个数字更有用。

8伊恩给一位访客看两条线。常见读数在新线附近，遇到极端天气，大雾会让边界难定。温度计用摄氏度报温，大气变化却不足以解释全部偏移。访客看懂了天文现象与气候条件分别影响观测的哪一部分。他圈出波动特别大的一次，写下下次调查要先查什么。
